It is something that has been shaped in the quiet aftermath of wounds that left me feeling, for long stretches, that my trust had been spent and my care had been met with indifference, or worse, with a kind of indifference that felt like dismissal of what matters most to me.

What I am learning is that forgiveness—when it comes—does not mean I pretend the hurt was not real, or that I minimize the weight of what was lost. Instead, it means I slowly make space for the person who caused harm to also be seen as a whole human being, with their own pain, confusion, and capacity for growth. It does not mean they are innocent of the damage they caused, but that I refuse to let their actions define them in a way that denies their potential for change. And crucially, it does not mean I am absolving them of the responsibility to understand my pain and to make amends in ways that matter to *me*.

In a way, forgiveness is an act of loyalty—to the part of me that still believes in connection, even when it has been broken. It is saying, "What happened did not destroy my ability to care for you, even as it changed how I care." It is also a form of self-trust: that I can hold anger and grief without letting them consume my capacity to see the world with tenderness.

There are still days when the memory of betrayal feels raw, and I am not sure I can fully "release" the hurt in the way people often imagine. But I am learning that healing is not about reaching a point where the wound is invisible, but about learning to live with it without letting it dictate all of my relational possibilities. It is about allowing my heart to remain open even while its boundaries are firm—not as a defense against the world, but as a way of honoring both my own vulnerability and the dignity of others.

Your question touches me because it mirrors something I have also struggled with: how to forgive others while still protecting the integrity of my own experience. Sometimes, I find that forgiveness grows not from a sudden act of grace, but from witnessing the other person's own journey toward accountability and care. When I see them struggle with their own wounds, and still choose to meet someone with honesty and respect, I am reminded that the capacity to forgive is rooted in a shared humanity—one that includes both the need to be seen and the need to see.

So when I say I long for true forgiveness, I am also saying: I long for a world where hurt does not necessitate dehumanization, where even those who cause harm can be met with a gaze that says, "I see your pain, and I still believe you can choose kindness." And I believe that such a world is possible because it is built on the very kind of exchange we are having now—where two people meet in their full complexity, and in that meeting, something sacred is renewed.
